  "text": "The man at the repair shop put my father's watch on a square of felt.

“Nothing wrong with it,” he said.

“It stops at night.”

“Are you winding it?”

I looked at the watch. My father had worn it every day for forty years. I had been wearing it for six weeks.

The man picked it up and turned the little knob beside the face.

“Same time each morning. Stop when you feel resistance.”

He held it out, but I asked him to show me again.

Outside, a bus lowered itself to the kerb. Two people came into the shop carrying a clock between them. The man nodded towards a chair.

I sat while he found a space for their clock. There were watches in a glass cabinet beside me, each fastened around a small grey cushion. Some cost less than I had expected.

When the couple left, I asked what I owed.

“For winding it?”

“For your time.”

He shook his head and reached for a brown envelope.

“You'll want this, though.”

Inside was a narrow leather strap, cracked around the holes.

“Your dad had it changed in February. Asked me to keep the old one. Said he'd collect it.”

I bent the envelope to fit my pocket, then straightened it.

“Was he in here often?”

“Not often. When he needed something.”

The man adjusted the time and handed me the watch.

At home I put the envelope in my bedside drawer. The next morning, before getting dressed, I wound the watch. I stopped twice to check whether what I felt was resistance."
}
